title: AI Detectors in College Classrooms
author: Sydney Sharkey
summary: A college instructor explores the growing practice of connecting AI detectors such as Turnitin and Pangram to Canvas assignments and asks what colleges are really trying to detect. She grants that the worry is real, pointing to falling twelfth-grade reading scores, but argues that surveillance damages the trust that learning relies on, citing research linking faculty-student rapport to deeper learning. Drawing on motivation research and a critique of market-driven higher education, she warns that reading and writing become transactional when completion and grades dominate. She notes that Stanford researchers found detectors misclassifying non-native English writing and concludes that a probability score cannot replace a conversation about a student's process. Her alternative is more drafts, conferences, in-class writing and revision histories, along with open talk about what college is for. The essay is explicitly exploratory and admits that no definitive answer exists.
points: Detectors push students to focus on avoiding suspicion rather than on learning, which erodes the instructor-student relationship that supports deep engagement.
Stanford research found widely used detectors flagged more than half of TOEFL essays by non-native speakers as AI-written, so a detector score is weak evidence of misconduct.
Reading and writing can become transactional when courses revolve around completion and grades, and AI makes it easy to bypass the struggle where learning happens.
Evaluating process through drafts, conferences, in-class writing and revision histories shows more about student thinking than a detector report does.
Instructors should discuss openly with students what college is for, because an assignment aimed only at a polished document invites the shortcut.
quotes: If students believe their instructor is primarily trying to catch them, they may become more focused on avoiding detection than on developing intellectual independence. The question becomes not “What did I learn?” but “Will this look suspicious?
A probability score is not a substitute for a conversation with a student. If a detector identifies a concern, perhaps the appropriate response is to ask the student about their process.
A student who struggles through a confusing article is practicing interpretation. A student who drafts an awkward paragraph is learning how to make an idea visible to someone else.

That may require placing greater emphasis on drafts, conferences, in-class writing, reflections, source annotations, and revision histories. These practices require more time than clicking on a detector report, but they also tell us more about how students think.

Ultimately, I think we need to talk more directly with students about what college is for. If the purpose of an assignment is only to produce a polished document, then artificial intelligence may seem like a reasonable shortcut.
I am not convinced that the future of education will be secured by more surveillance. I am also not convinced that unrestricted access to AI will automatically produce better learning.
